questions.q: In the scenario, why does the architect recommend moving 14 fields to an extension table instead of deleting them?
options: Because ServiceNow does not allow fields to ever be deleted
Because a handful of old reports still reference them, so moving them off the base table reduces width without losing access entirely
Because extension tables are always faster than base tables regardless of content
Because the 14 fields are the most frequently used fields on the table
questions.explain: The 14 fields are rarely used but not unused — moving them to a related extension table narrows the base table while preserving access for the reports that still need them.

questions.q: What confirmed fact drives the specific 3-year archiving policy in this scenario, rather than an arbitrary cutoff?
options: A guess that 3 years sounds reasonable for most companies
The organization's confirmed compliance obligation requiring records to remain available for 3 years after closure, with no requirement to stay in the live table beyond that
A ServiceNow platform limit on how long incidents can stay active
A decision made without checking with the compliance team
questions.explain: Per lesson 9's guidance, the policy is grounded in a confirmed, verified retention requirement, not an assumed or arbitrary number.

questions.q: Why does archiving incidents more than 3 years old create a CSDM/CMDB governance issue in this scenario?
options: Archiving automatically deletes the CMDB CI relationship entirely
A CI's "recent incidents" view, if it only queries the active table, silently stops showing anything older than 3 years, which can look like the CI had no problems
It has no effect on CMDB-facing views at all
CMDB relationships cannot exist on archived records
questions.explain: The incident-to-CI relationship survives archiving, but a view that only queries the active table will silently omit archived incidents — creating a misleading impression unless it's addressed.

questions.q: What is the actual governance fix the lesson recommends for the CMDB-visibility gap, rather than blocking the archiving policy?
options: Relabel CMDB-facing incident-history views to state their real time window, and document the rule for future reporting work
Cancel the archiving policy entirely to avoid the issue
Delete all CMDB relationships on archived incidents
Ignore the issue since it only affects a small number of reports
questions.explain: The fix makes the limitation explicit and owned — relabeling views and documenting the rule — rather than quietly leaving a misleading impression or abandoning the performance fix.

questions.q: Why does this lab treat table width, archiving, and CSDM governance as one combined decision rather than three separate fixes?
options: Because ServiceNow requires all three to be configured in a single change request
Because the archiving decision made for query performance has a direct, traceable consequence on CMDB-facing CSDM reporting that has to be accounted for, not treated in isolation
Because table width has no real connection to archiving or CSDM
Because this is simply a stylistic choice with no architectural reasoning behind it
questions.explain: The lab's core lesson is that these architecture decisions interact — an archiving policy built purely for performance has real downstream effects on CMDB visibility that an architect has to trace and own.
